title: Java LinkedList
learningObjectives: Create a LinkedList using the List or Deque interface.
Add and remove elements at both ends.
Select LinkedList when queue or deque operations fit the task.

understand.concept: LinkedList is a doubly linked implementation of List and Deque. Each element is stored in a node linked to its neighbours. It supports efficient insertion and removal at the ends, and can act as a queue or deque. Indexed access requires traversal, so it is generally slower than ArrayList for frequent random reads. Choose a collection based on the operations the program performs rather than assuming one is always faster.
understand.whyItMatters: This topic helps Java developers select and use the right standard-library tools for java linkedlist in maintainable applications.
understand.analogy: Think of the collection or date API as a purpose-built tool: its operations communicate the guarantees your program can rely on.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only a guide; Java API contracts, equality rules and exception behaviour determine the actual result.

explain.narrative: LinkedList implements both List and Deque. Methods such as addFirst, addLast, getFirst, removeFirst and peekLast express end operations clearly. As a queue, offer adds and poll retrieves/removes the head. A Deque supports both ends and can model a queue or stack. Be careful with methods that throw when empty, such as getFirst; peekFirst returns null instead. The data structure choice should follow access patterns and measured needs.

examples.title: Add at both ends
examples.code:
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { LinkedList<String> line = new LinkedList<>(); line.add("B"); line.addFirst("A"); line.addLast("C"); System.out.println(line); } }
examples.explanation: LinkedList offers methods for inserting at either end.

examples.title: Read the ends
examples.code:
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { LinkedList<Integer> q = new LinkedList<>(); q.add(10); q.add(20); System.out.println(q.getFirst()); System.out.println(q.getLast()); } }
examples.explanation: getFirst and getLast inspect the two ends.

examples.title: Remove the first item
examples.code:
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { LinkedList<String> q = new LinkedList<>(); q.add("Job1"); q.add("Job2"); System.out.println(q.removeFirst()); System.out.println(q); } }
examples.explanation: removeFirst removes and returns the head element.

examples.title: Use as a queue
examples.code:
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { LinkedList<String> q = new LinkedList<>(); q.offer("Print"); q.offer("Scan"); System.out.println(q.poll()); System.out.println(q.peek()); } }
examples.explanation: offer, poll and peek are queue-style operations.

examples.title: Traverse in order
examples.code:
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { LinkedList<Integer> nums = new LinkedList<>(); nums.add(3); nums.add(6); nums.add(9); for (int n : nums) System.out.print(n + " "); } }
examples.explanation: Enhanced for preserves the linked list's insertion order.
